passages.t: Ziklag burned, and strength in the LORD
passages.happening:
On the third day David and his men reach Ziklag. The Amalekites have raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag and burned it (verse 1). They have taken captive the women and everyone else, young and old. ‘They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way’ (verse 2).

David and his men find the town burned and their wives, sons and daughters gone. ‘So David and the troops with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep’ (verse 4). David's two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, have been taken too (verse 5).

“And David was greatly distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God” (verse 6).

He tells Abiathar the priest to bring the ephod, and he asks the LORD whether to pursue the raiders and whether he will catch them (verses 7-8). “Pursue them,” the LORD replied, “for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
While the Philistines and Israel prepare for battle at Gilboa, the story follows David south. He has been spared from fighting Israel, but he comes home to disaster. The Amalekite raid turns his own raids of chapter 27 back on him. Now it is his town that is stripped and his family that is taken.

The Amalekites were a half-wandering people of the southern deserts, remembered as Israel's first enemy after the exodus. Saul's failure to deal with them as the LORD commanded was the reason he was rejected. The raiders struck while the fighting men of the south were away with the armies. They took captives rather than killing them, probably to sell as slaves, which is why the families could still be found.

Stoning was how a community put to death someone judged guilty of a grave wrong. The men's talk of stoning David shows how far their grief had turned into blame against their leader. It is the lowest point of David's outlaw years.

Then comes the hinge of the chapter. David finds strength in the LORD his God. His strength does not come from his circumstances, which are ruined, but from God. And for the first time since he went over to the Philistines, he asks the LORD before he acts. He asks two plain questions and gets a plain answer: pursue.
passages.later: The same word for taking strength is in God's charge to Joshua: “Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9).
passages.asks: When everything was gone and his own men turned on him, David found strength in the LORD his God. Ask where you turn when every human support gives way. And ask whether you, like David, need to start asking God again after a long stretch of deciding alone.

passages.t: The pursuit, and an Egyptian left to die
passages.happening:
David sets out with six hundred men. At the Brook of Besor two hundred are too exhausted to cross, and they stay behind. David goes on with four hundred (verses 9-10).

His men find an Egyptian in a field and bring him to David. They give him water and food, a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins, and he revives, for he has eaten nothing for three days and nights (verses 11-12). He is the slave of an Amalekite. ‘My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill’ (verse 13). He was with the raiders who burned Ziklag (verse 14). If David will swear not to kill him or hand him back to his master, he will lead him to them (verse 15).

He leads David down, and there are the Amalekites spread over the land, eating, drinking and celebrating their plunder (verse 16). David strikes them from twilight to the evening of the next day. Only four hundred young men escape on camels (verse 17).

David recovers everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. ‘Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken. David brought everything back’ (verse 19). His men drive the flocks ahead, calling out, “This is David’s plunder!” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The Brook of Besor is a seasonal streambed in the northwest of the Negev, usually identified with the valley now called Nahal Besor, which drains toward the coast near Gaza.

The Egyptian slave shows both the harshness and the hospitality of the desert. His master left him to die when he fell ill, a cheap reckoning about a sick slave. David's men feed him first and question him afterward. He asks for an oath that he will be neither killed nor handed back, and he becomes the guide who leads them to the camp.

The Cherethites, whose southern lands the raiders struck, were a people linked with the Philistines and probably with Crete. Men from this people later served in David's bodyguard.

The chapter moves from total loss to total recovery, and the narrator presses the point by repeating it: nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter. The numbers carry the story too. Six hundred set out, two hundred drop out, four hundred fight, and exactly four hundred Amalekites escape.

While Saul, who failed to carry out the LORD's judgment on Amalek, is about to die, David is defeating Amalek.
passages.later:
Isaiah names this kind of mercy among the things God asks of his people: ‘to share your bread with the hungry’ (Isaiah 58:7).

Men of the Cherethites later guarded David as king: ‘Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites’ (2 Samuel 8:18).
passages.asks: David's men fed a sick, abandoned slave before they asked him anything. Ask who has been left behind in the field near you, and whether you stop for them. And ask what it would mean to recover everything that was lost, as David did, and to give God the credit for it.

passages.t: Equal shares, and gifts for Judah
passages.happening:
David comes back to the two hundred men who were too exhausted to go on, and greets them (verse 21). ‘But all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David’ say that those who stayed behind will get none of the plunder, only their wives and children (verse 22).

David answers, “My brothers, you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us” (verse 23). “The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike” (verse 24). ‘David established this statute as an ordinance for Israel to this very day’ (verse 25).

When he reaches Ziklag, he sends part of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah: “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies” (verse 26). He sends gifts to many towns of the south, ‘and to those in Hebron and in all the places where David and his men had roamed’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The word for plunder appears again and again in this chapter, and how it is shared shows the character of those who share it. The Amalekites feast on it. David's men shout that it is David's plunder. The worthless men want to keep it from the weary. David says it is what the LORD has given.

The word for worthless is the word used of Eli's corrupt sons and of Nabal. Here it describes men whose greed would split the community.

Israel's law had already said that plunder should be divided between those who fought and the rest of the people. David goes further: the men who guarded the baggage share equally with those who fought. His ruling rests on grace. What the LORD has given cannot be hoarded by the strong. It is David's first act of lawgiving, and it becomes a lasting rule, the act of a king before he wears the crown.

The gifts to the elders of Judah shared the victory with the towns that had sheltered him, and prepared their loyalty. The towns lie across the southern hill country and the Negev. The Bethel in this list is probably a southern town of that name, not the Bethel north of Jerusalem. The chapter closes on the name Hebron, where David will be crowned.
passages.later:
The law of Moses had commanded a division of plunder: ‘Then divide the captives between the troops who went out to battle and the rest of the congregation’ (Numbers 31:27).

The next part of the story begins with the men of these towns: ‘Then the men of Judah came to Hebron, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah’ (2 Samuel 2:4).
passages.asks: David would not let the strong keep the gift from the weary. Ask who in your church or family has been too tired to go into the battle, and whether they share in what God has given. And ask whether you think of what you have as earned, or as given.
